subject: Government
title: The State, Nation, and Society
outline: Meaning and features of a state
Theories of the origin of the state
Functions and end of the state

modules.title: The Four Essential Elements of a State
modules.html:
A state is a politically organised body of people occupying a definite territory, under a government, and free from external control. Four elements must be present together; the absence of any one means the entity is not a state.

ElementExplanationNote
PopulationA permanent body of people living together.No minimum number is fixed; the Vatican has fewer than 1,000 citizens.
TerritoryA defined geographical area including land, territorial waters and airspace.Boundaries need not be undisputed, only identifiable.
GovernmentThe machinery that formulates and enforces the collective will.Form is irrelevant – monarchy, republic or military regime.
SovereigntySupreme legal authority internally and independence externally.The decisive element; a colony has the first three but not this.

Permanence is sometimes added as a fifth feature: the state outlives any particular government or generation. Governments change every four years in Nigeria; the Nigerian state persists.

examples.q: Why was colonial Nigeria (1914–1960) not a state?
examples.a: It had population, territory and a government, but sovereignty resided in Britain. Lacking independence, it was a dependency, not a state.

modules.title: State, Nation and Nation-State
modules.html:
A nation is a group of people bound together by a sense of common identity — shared language, culture, history, religion or ancestry — and a will to live together. It is a sociological and psychological concept, whereas the state is a legal and political one.

BasisStateNation
NatureLegal and political entity.Cultural and psychological entity.
Essential elementSovereignty.Common consciousness and identity.
TerritoryMust have a defined territory.May have no territory (e.g. the Kurds).
MembershipAll who owe allegiance, including naturalised aliens.Those who share the culture and sentiment.
ForceCan lawfully compel obedience.Relies on sentiment, not coercion.

Where the boundaries of the nation coincide with those of the state, we have a nation-state (Japan, Iceland, Somalia approximately). Where many nations live within one state we have a multi-national or multi-ethnic state — Nigeria, with more than 250 ethnic groups, is the classic African example. Conversely one nation may be spread across several states, as with the Yoruba in Nigeria, Benin and Togo.

examples.a: Strictly, no. Nigeria is a multi-national state: over 250 ethnic nations (Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, Ijaw, Tiv and others) live within one sovereign state. Nation-building policies such as NYSC and the federal character principle aim to forge a single Nigerian nation.

modules.title: Society, Association and the State
modules.html:
Society is the widest grouping of human beings living together and interacting for the satisfaction of their needs. It embraces the family, the school, the market, the church and the state itself. Society is therefore older and wider than the state.

An association is an organised group formed for a specific purpose — the Nigerian Bar Association, a cooperative society, a football club. Compare the three:

  • Membership: compulsory in the state; voluntary in an association; automatic in society.
  • Purpose: the state pursues the general welfare; an association pursues a limited aim; society covers the whole of social life.
  • Sanction: only the state may lawfully use force; an association may only expel a member.

Because the state alone possesses the monopoly of legitimate force (Max Weber), it stands above all other associations within its territory.

examples.q: Give one reason why membership of a state differs from membership of a club.
examples.a: Membership of a state is compulsory – one is born into it and cannot simply resign – while club membership is voluntary and may be ended at will.

modules.title: Theories of the Origin of the State
modules.html:
Four theories are examined at this level.

  1. Divine Right Theory: the state was created by God and the ruler is God's deputy, answerable only to God. Popular in medieval Europe (King James I of England, Louis XIV of France). Criticised as unverifiable and a licence for tyranny.
  2. Social Contract Theory: the state arose from an agreement among people to escape the state of nature. Thomas Hobbes described life in the state of nature as “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short” and surrendered all rights to an absolute sovereign; John Locke saw the state of nature as tolerable and surrendered only limited powers, retaining life, liberty and property, with a right of revolt; Jean-Jacques Rousseau based the state on the general will of the people.
  3. Force Theory: the state grew out of conquest — the strong subdued the weak. Explains the growth of empires such as the Oyo and Sokoto, but cannot explain voluntary allegiance.
  4. Evolutionary (Natural/Patriarchal) Theory: the state grew gradually from the family to the clan, the village and the kingdom. Aristotle's dictum that “man is by nature a political animal” supports this view, which most scholars accept.

examples.q: Which social contract theorist justified the right of the people to overthrow a bad government?
examples.a: John Locke. Because the contract was limited and conditional, a ruler who violates natural rights breaks the trust and may lawfully be resisted.

modules.title: Meaning and features of a state
modules.html:
Meaning and features of a state is a key part of The State, Nation, and Society (SSS 1, Government). Master the meaning, the main points and how it is tested in JAMB and WAEC questions on this topic.

Key points

  • A state is a politically organised body of people occupying a definite territory, under a government, and free from external control.
  • Four elements must be present together; the absence of any one means the entity is not a state.
  • Permanence is sometimes added as a fifth feature: the state outlives any particular government or generation.
  • Governments change every four years in Nigeria; the Nigerian state persists.
  • It is a sociological and psychological concept, whereas the state is a legal and political one.

Worked example

Q: Which element distinguishes a state from a colony?
A: Sovereignty — A colony has the other three but its sovereignty lies elsewhere.

Q: Nigeria is best described as a
A: Multi-national state — Over 250 ethnic nations live within one Nigerian state.

examples.a: Sovereignty — A colony has the other three but its sovereignty lies elsewhere.

examples.q: Nigeria is best described as a
examples.a: Multi-national state — Over 250 ethnic nations live within one Nigerian state.
